articles.title: Is my baby ready for solids?
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] The signs to look for, and why about 6 months is the usual start.

sections.heading: When to start
paragraphs: Most babies are ready for foods other than breast milk or formula at about 6 months. Starting before 4 months isn't recommended. Every baby is different, so look at your baby, not just the calendar.
From 6 to 12 months, breast milk or formula is still the main source of nutrition. Solid foods gradually become a bigger part of the diet.

sections.heading: Signs your baby is ready
paragraphs: Look for these signs together:
bullets: Sits up alone or with support
Can control their head and neck
Opens their mouth when you offer food
Swallows food rather than pushing it back out onto their chin
Brings objects to their mouth
Tries to grasp small objects, such as toys or food
Moves food from the front to the back of the tongue to swallow

sections.heading: If the first tries don't go well
paragraphs: If your baby pushes the food out and it dribbles down their chin, they may not be able to move it to the back of their mouth yet. That's normal: they've never had anything thicker than milk.
Try thinning the food the first few times, then gradually thicken it. Or wait a week or two and try again. If your baby cries or turns away, don't make them eat.

sections.heading: Babies born early
paragraphs: If your baby was born early, ask your pediatrician when to start. This app counts your baby's age from their due date (corrected age) where that applies.

articles.title: Choosing and using a high chair
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] What to look for when you buy one, and how to use it safely at every meal.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: High chairs are linked to thousands of emergency room visits each year. Most injuries happen when a child climbs in or out, when the chair tips as a child pushes back or rocks, or when a part like the strap, tray or lock fails.

sections.heading: What to look for
bullets: A chair that can't be tipped over easily.
A manufacture date on or after June 19, 2019. Chairs made since then must meet a federal standard for stability, restraints and warning labels. The date is on a label on the chair.
If it folds, a lock that holds every time you set it up.
Straps that include a crotch strap, not just a waist strap.
For a secondhand chair, check that it hasn't been recalled at CPSC.gov.

sections.heading: At every meal
bullets: Use the safety straps every time, including the crotch strap, and adjust them to fit snugly. This stops your baby from slipping down.
Don't rely on the tray to hold your baby in. It isn't a restraint.
Never let your child stand in the high chair.
Keep the chair away from counters and tables; a child can push off hard enough to tip it.
Never leave your baby alone in the chair, and don't let older children climb or play on it.

sections.heading: Hook-on chairs
paragraphs: A chair that hooks onto a table isn't a good substitute for a freestanding one. If you use one when eating out or traveling, choose one that locks onto the table, make sure the table is heavy enough not to tip, and check that your child's feet can't push against a table support.

articles.title: Purees or finger foods?
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] How textures build up, and how spoon-feeding and finger foods fit together.

sections.heading: Start smooth
paragraphs: At around 6 months, it's easiest for babies to eat very smooth mashed, pureed or strained foods. It can take time to adjust to new textures, and your baby may cough, gag or spit up while learning.

sections.heading: Then build up textures
paragraphs: As your baby's skills develop, move on to thicker and lumpier foods, then finely chopped or ground foods. Trying different textures helps your baby:
bullets: Learn to accept and like a variety of foods
Develop fine motor skills, like pinching and picking up food
Develop chewing skills

sections.heading: When finger foods fit in
paragraphs: Once your baby can sit up and bring their hands or objects to their mouth, they can start feeding themselves finger foods. Choose foods that are soft, easy to swallow and cut into small pieces, for example:
bullets: Small pieces of banana
Scrambled eggs
Well-cooked pasta
Well-cooked, finely chopped chicken
Well-cooked, cut-up potatoes or peas
Small pieces of soft bread

sections.heading: You don't have to choose
paragraphs: Spoon-feeding and finger foods work well together. Many babies eat purees from a spoon while they practice picking up soft pieces. By about 12 months, most babies can easily feed themselves with their fingers.

sections.heading: Whichever way you go
bullets: Offer foods that dissolve easily or don't need chewing, cut small.
Sit your baby upright, and stay with them the whole meal.
Keep meals calm and unhurried.

articles.title: What to offer first
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] There's no set order, but iron-rich foods matter from the start.

sections.heading: Any order works
paragraphs: For most babies, foods don't need to come in a certain order. There's no evidence that offering fruit first makes a baby dislike vegetables.

sections.heading: Put iron first
paragraphs: From about 6 months, your baby needs iron and zinc from food. Include foods like:
bullets: Pureed meat, poultry or fish
Iron-fortified infant cereal
Eggs
Beans, lentils and tofu

sections.heading: One at a time
paragraphs: Offer one single-ingredient food at a time, and wait 3 to 5 days before the next new food. That makes it easier to spot a reaction.

sections.heading: Build variety
paragraphs: By 7 or 8 months, many babies are eating foods from every group: vegetables, fruits, proteins, dairy without added sugar, and whole grains.
If you use infant cereal, rotate oat, barley and multigrain rather than only rice cereal, which can raise arsenic exposure.

articles.title: Introducing common allergens
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Why offering egg, peanut and other allergens early can help, and how to do it.

sections.heading: Early can help
paragraphs: Experts used to suggest waiting. Newer research found no benefit to delaying allergens, and offering peanut early, then regularly, helped prevent peanut allergy in babies at high risk.

sections.heading: How to start
bullets: Start with a few low-allergy foods first, like infant cereal or pureed fruit.
Then offer the common allergens one at a time: egg, peanut, dairy (like yogurt), wheat, soy, sesame, fish, shellfish and tree nuts.
Start with a small taste. If there's no reaction, gradually offer more.
Once a food is tolerated, keep it in the diet regularly.
Always use a safe form: peanut and nut butters thinned, never chunks or whole nuts; egg fully cooked.

sections.heading: Talk to your pediatrician first if
bullets: Your baby has severe, persistent eczema
Your baby has had an allergic reaction to a food, such as egg

sections.heading: Watch for reactions
paragraphs: After a new food, watch for signs like a rash, vomiting or diarrhea. If you see them, stop the food and call your pediatrician. Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the lips or tongue, repeated vomiting, or unusual sleepiness.
Most egg allergies are caused by proteins in the egg white, but the yolk can cause reactions too.

articles.title: Gagging or choking?
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Gagging is part of learning to eat. Choking is an emergency. Know the difference.

sections.heading: Gagging is normal
paragraphs: While your baby learns new textures, coughing, sputtering and gagging are common. Stay calm, and keep them sitting upright.

sections.heading: Choking is an emergency
paragraphs: Choking happens when food or an object blocks the airway. Call 911 if your child:
bullets: Can't breathe, or is gasping or wheezing
Can't cry or make a sound
Turns a bluish color
Grabs at their throat or looks panicked
Goes limp or unconscious

sections.heading: Prevent it
bullets: Serve the right texture for your baby's stage.
Cut round foods like grapes into small pieces, and long foods like hot dogs into short, thin strips.
Have your baby sit upright to eat; no eating while lying down, crawling, walking, or in the car or stroller.
Always watch your baby while they eat.

sections.heading: Be ready
paragraphs: Ask your pediatrician what to do if your child chokes, and consider a certified infant CPR and first-aid class. The American Red Cross and American Heart Association offer them.

articles.title: Hungry or full?
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] How babies tell you they want more, or they're done.

sections.heading: Signs of hunger
paragraphs: From 6 months, your baby may be hungry if they:
bullets: Reach for or point to food
Open their mouth when offered a spoon or food
Get excited when they see food
Use hand motions or sounds to say they want more

sections.heading: Signs of fullness
bullets: Push food away
Close their mouth when food is offered
Turn their head away
Use hand motions or sounds to say they're done

sections.heading: Let them decide
paragraphs: Your baby doesn't need to finish the jar or the plate. Food works best when it isn't used as a reward or punishment. If you're worried about how much your baby eats, talk to your pediatrician.

articles.title: Cups, water and juice
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] When to offer a cup, how much water, and why juice can wait.

sections.heading: A first cup
paragraphs: From about 6 months, you can offer a cup with a spouted lid, a cup with a straw, or an open cup. Around 9 months, babies can start learning to drink from a cup without a lid; by 12 months they can drink from one as you hold it. Expect spills.

sections.heading: Water
paragraphs: Breast milk or formula gives your baby the fluids they need. Once solids start, a little water is fine: about 4 to 8 oz a day.

sections.heading: Juice
paragraphs: Juice isn't recommended before 12 months. After that, if you offer it, give only 100% juice, no more than 4 oz a day, in a cup, not a bottle.

sections.heading: Cow's milk
paragraphs: Plain cow's milk as a drink waits until 12 months.

articles.title: Making and storing baby food
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] A few hours of prep can stock your freezer for weeks.

sections.heading: Make it
paragraphs: Pick some fruits, vegetables and grains. Cook them until soft enough to mash easily with a fork; ripe banana and avocado can be mashed raw. Puree or mash, and thin with breast milk, formula or water.
bullets: Cook with no added salt or seasoning.
Remove fat, skin and bones from meat, poultry and fish before cooking.
Remove seeds and hard pits from fruit.

sections.heading: Store it
paragraphs: Homemade food isn't bacteria-free and spoils faster than food from a jar. Refrigerate what you don't use and check for signs of spoilage before serving.
To freeze, spoon purees into ice-cube trays. Once frozen, move the cubes to labeled, dated bags and use them within 3 months. Later, mix cubes to make new combinations.

articles.title: Foods to skip in the first year
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Honey, added sugar and a few others that wait until later.

sections.heading: Not before 12 months
bullets: Honey, in any form. It can cause infant botulism, a severe food poisoning.
Cow's milk or plant milks as a drink.
Juice.

sections.heading: Not for babies or toddlers
bullets: Added sugars, including sweetened yogurts, cookies and sweet drinks.
Salty foods. Choose canned foods labeled low sodium or no salt added.
Unpasteurized (raw) milk, cheese, yogurt or juice.
Fish high in mercury, like shark, swordfish and king mackerel.

sections.heading: Choking hazards
paragraphs: Some foods are only safe once changed: whole grapes, nuts, chunks of nut butter, raw hard vegetables and more. See the choking guide in this tab.

articles.title: When your baby refuses food
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Refusing new foods is normal. Here's how to keep offering.

sections.heading: It takes time
paragraphs: Your baby may not like a food the first time. It can take 8 to 10 tries before a young child accepts a new food.

sections.heading: Try this
bullets: Wait about a week, then offer the food again.
Mix the new food with one your baby already likes.
Eat the food yourself first; babies learn by watching.
Give a simple choice between two foods.
Freeze small portions so repeat tries don't waste food.

sections.heading: Phases are normal
paragraphs: Toddlers may suddenly refuse foods they used to love, or not want foods to touch. These phases often pass by about age 5. Talk to your pediatrician if you're worried about growth.

articles.title: Moving to cow's milk
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] What changes at 12 months, and how much is enough.

sections.heading: Why wait until 12 months
paragraphs: Before 12 months, cow's milk as a drink may cause intestinal bleeding, has too much protein and minerals for a baby's kidneys, and lacks the right nutrients.

sections.heading: What to offer
paragraphs: From 12 months, offer plain, pasteurized whole cow's milk, or a plant milk fortified with calcium and vitamin D, unflavored and unsweetened. Children 12 to 23 months need about 2 servings of dairy a day, which can include milk, full-fat yogurt and cheese.

sections.heading: Not too much
paragraphs: Milk is a drink, not a replacement for food. Too much can leave your child less hungry for other foods, and some experts say it can make it harder to absorb iron. Ask your pediatrician if you're unsure how much is right.

articles.title: Physical healing and postpartum recovery
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Beyond the 6-week checkup: what's happening in your body, how to look after it, and when to get help.

sections.heading: Healing takes longer than 6 weeks
paragraphs: Many moms feel they should be back to normal by the 6-week checkup. In reality, your body keeps healing for months after birth, and that's expected. Go easy on yourself.
Your postpartum visit is a good time to bring up anything that still hurts, leaks or worries you. You don't have to wait for it: if something feels wrong, call your OB-GYN or midwife.
Get medical care right away, or call 911, if you have any of these warning signs in the year after birth:
bullets: Heavy bleeding: soaking through one or more pads in an hour, or passing clots bigger than an egg
A fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher
A headache that won't go away or gets worse, or changes in your vision
Trouble breathing, chest pain, or a racing heartbeat
Swelling, redness or pain in one leg or arm
Severe belly pain that doesn't go away
Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby

sections.heading: Pelvic floor and core
paragraphs: Pregnancy and birth stretch the muscles that support your bladder, uterus and bowel (your pelvic floor), and the muscles down the middle of your belly. They usually get stronger again with time and gentle exercise.
Pelvic floor exercises (Kegels) can usually start soon after birth. To do one, squeeze the muscles you use to hold in pee, hold for a moment, then relax.

After an uncomplicated vaginal birth, many moms can start gentle activity like walking as soon as they feel able. After a C-section, full activity usually comes back around 4 to 6 weeks if there are no complications. Check with your provider before you start, and build up slowly.

Some moms notice a gap or a ridge down the middle of the belly when they sit up. This is called diastasis recti and is common after pregnancy. Ask your provider or a pelvic floor physical therapist which exercises are right for you.
bullets: See your provider if you feel pressure or heaviness in your pelvis or vagina, or feel something bulging at the vaginal opening. These can be signs of prolapse.
Leaking pee, low back ache, or symptoms that get worse when you stand or lift are worth mentioning too.
Ask for a referral to a pelvic floor physical therapist if you have any of these, or if you're not sure you're doing the exercises right.

sections.heading: The hormonal rollercoaster
paragraphs: Your hormones shift quickly after birth. Many moms have night sweats in the first weeks, and skin changes from pregnancy often fade slowly over the following months.
Hair shedding is common too. It usually peaks about 4 months after birth, and most moms have their normal hair growth back by their child's first birthday.
In the first few days after birth, many moms have mood swings, sadness, anxiety, crying spells or trouble sleeping. This is often called the baby blues, and it usually passes within a few days.
Postpartum depression is different: it's stronger and lasts longer than 2 weeks. About 1 in 8 new moms have symptoms in the year after birth. It's common, it's not your fault, and it can be treated.
bullets: Talk to your provider if low mood, worry or tiredness lasts longer than 2 weeks or makes it hard to care for yourself or your baby.
National Maternal Mental Health Hotline: call or text 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262), free, 24/7.
In a crisis, call or text 988. If you or your baby are in danger, call 911.

sections.heading: Caring for a tear or stitches
paragraphs: A tear or an episiotomy can take many weeks to heal. Stitches usually dissolve on their own.
Wait 6 weeks before using tampons or having sex, unless your provider tells you otherwise.
bullets: Ice packs help with pain and swelling in the first 24 hours.
After 24 hours, warm sitz baths can soothe the area.
After you pee or poop, spray warm water over the area and pat it dry.
Change pads every 2 to 4 hours.
Drink plenty of water and eat high-fiber foods to keep stools soft. Ask about a stool softener if you need one.
Ask your provider which pain relievers are safe for you, especially if you're breastfeeding.

sections.heading: Caring for a C-section incision
paragraphs: A C-section is major surgery, so give yourself time. Many moms need several weeks before they feel like themselves again.
Once your incision has fully closed, ask your provider or a physical therapist whether scar massage is right for you.
bullets: Don't lift anything heavier than your baby for the first 6 to 8 weeks.
Care for the dressing the way your care team showed you.
Showers are usually fine. Wait for your provider's OK before soaking in a bath or hot tub, or swimming.
Call your provider if the incision gets red, warm, swollen or starts to drain, smells bad, or opens, or if your pain gets worse.

sections.heading: Food for recovery
paragraphs: Your body is healing and, if you're breastfeeding, making milk too. Regular meals with a mix of foods help you keep going. Breastfeeding moms need about 330 to 400 extra calories a day.
Your needs for some nutrients, like iodine and choline, go up while you breastfeed. Eggs, dairy, meat and low-mercury fish are good sources.
Ask your provider whether you should keep taking a prenatal vitamin or another supplement. If you lost a lot of blood at birth, ask whether you need extra iron.
If cooking feels like too much, that's normal. Simple, one-handed meals count.
bullets: Eggs, yogurt and cheese
Beans, lentils and whole grains for fiber
Lots of fruits and vegetables
Lean meat and poultry
Low-mercury fish like salmon, 2 to 3 servings a week
Water within reach whenever you sit down

articles.title: Infant sleep and feeding realities
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Survival strategies for the first months: feeding your way, what newborn sleep really looks like, and how to keep sleep safe.

sections.heading: Feeding your baby, your way
paragraphs: Breast milk, formula or both: a fed, loved baby is the goal. Whatever you choose, and however it changes over time, you deserve support, not judgment.
Newborns feed often. Most feed 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, as often as every 1 to 3 hours, including at night. That's tiring, and it's normal.

sections.heading: Breastfeeding (or chestfeeding) realities
paragraphs: A good latch is key. Your baby should take in most of the darker skin around the nipple (the areola), not just the nipple. If it hurts or your baby is only on the nipple, slide a clean finger into the corner of their mouth to break the suction and try again.

In the first days your breasts may feel very full, hard or sore (engorgement). It usually eases as your body adjusts. Feeding often, hand expressing or pumping a little to soften the breast before a feed, and cold packs between feeds can help.

Pain is a sign to get help early, not to push through. A breastfeeding specialist (look for an IBCLC), your pediatrician or your OB-GYN can check the latch and look at things like tongue tie. Ask them before deciding on any treatment.
bullets: Call your doctor if part of your breast is red, warm or painful and you have a fever or flu-like aches. These can be signs of mastitis, a breast infection.
Get care right away for red streaks on the breast, pus or blood in your milk, both breasts affected, or symptoms that suddenly get much worse.
Also call if you don't feel better within 24 hours, or if feeding stays painful.

sections.heading: Weaning or switching to formula
paragraphs: Moving to formula, combining, or stopping breastfeeding can bring up big feelings: relief, guilt, sadness, or all three at once. Those feelings are common, and none of them mean you've failed.
Cutting back slowly is usually more comfortable for your body. A breastfeeding specialist can help you make a plan.
If low mood, worry or guilt lasts longer than 2 weeks, talk to your provider, or call or text the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline at 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262).

sections.heading: Formula feeding and combo feeding
paragraphs: All infant formula sold legally in the US is reviewed by the FDA to make sure it meets nutrition and safety requirements. No brand is best, and store brands are held to the same rules. Iron-fortified formula is recommended.
Combo feeding, giving both breast milk and formula, is a real option that works for many families. Talk with your pediatrician about how to fit it together for your baby.
bullets: Mix formula exactly as the label says. Never add extra water to stretch it.
Don't make homemade formula, and don't use formula labeled for toddlers before 12 months.
Check that cans aren't expired, dented, puffy or leaking.
Ask your pediatrician before switching brands or types, especially for special formulas.

sections.heading: A pumping routine you can live with
paragraphs: There's no single right pumping schedule. Fit it around your baby's feeds, your work and your sleep, and ask a breastfeeding specialist to help you make it manageable.
Storing milk safely takes the pressure off. These are the CDC's guidelines for freshly pumped milk:
bullets: Room temperature (77°F or cooler): up to 4 hours
Refrigerator (40°F or colder): up to 4 days
Freezer (0°F or colder): best within 6 months, up to 12 months
Thawed milk: use within 24 hours, and never refreeze it
Leftovers from a feeding: use within 2 hours, then throw them away
Freeze in small portions, about 2 to 4 oz, to waste less

sections.heading: What newborn sleep really looks like
paragraphs: Newborns sleep about 16 to 17 hours a day, but often only 1 or 2 hours at a time. They wake often because they need to eat, day and night.
Babies don't have regular sleep cycles until about 4 months. Longer stretches come gradually, and every baby gets there on their own timeline.

Strict wake-window charts and programs promising a newborn will sleep through the night aren't part of official US guidance. Be wary of anything that makes you feel your baby is broken: frequent waking is what newborns are built to do.
Things that can help: keep days bright and playful and nights calm, quiet and dim. From around 4 months, try putting your baby down drowsy but awake.

sections.heading: Safe sleep, every sleep
paragraphs: These steps lower the risk of SIDS and other sleep-related deaths. They apply to naps and nighttime alike.
bullets: Always place your baby on their back to sleep.
Use a firm, flat surface that isn't inclined, like a crib or bassinet with a fitted sheet.
Keep the sleep space empty: no pillows, blankets, bumpers or soft toys.
Share a room, not a bed, for at least the first 6 months.
Never sleep with your baby on a couch or armchair. It's far riskier than any other place.
If your baby falls asleep in a car seat, swing or carrier, move them to a firm, flat sleep surface on their back as soon as you can.
Swaddling doesn't lower the risk of SIDS. If you swaddle, stop as soon as your baby shows signs of trying to roll, often around 3 to 4 months.
Don't use weighted sleep sacks, swaddles or blankets.
Offering a pacifier at naps and bedtime can help. If you're breastfeeding, you can wait until feeding is going well.
Keep your baby from getting too hot, keep their head uncovered, and keep smoke and nicotine away from them.

sections.heading: When to call
paragraphs: Call your pediatrician if your baby seems hard to wake, isn't feeding well, has fewer wet diapers than usual, or you're worried. Trust your gut. In an emergency, call 911.

articles.title: Mental health and emotional wellbeing
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Giving words and grace to the invisible emotional load of new motherhood, and knowing when to reach out.

sections.heading: You're not alone, and it's not your fault
paragraphs: Becoming a mom changes everything at once: your body, your sleep, your relationships and how you see yourself. Big feelings are part of that, and they deserve care too.
If you're struggling, it's not because you did something wrong. Perinatal mental health conditions are medical conditions, they're common, and treatment and support work.
bullets: National Maternal Mental Health Hotline: call or text 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262), free, 24/7.
If you're thinking about hurting yourself or your baby, call or text 988 now.
If you or your baby are in danger, call 911.
If you're experiencing domestic violence: National Domestic Violence Hotline, 1-800-799-7233.

sections.heading: Beyond postpartum depression
paragraphs: In the first two weeks, many moms have the baby blues: mood swings, tears and worry that pass on their own. If feelings last longer than 2 weeks, or feel very intense, talk to your provider. Postpartum depression usually doesn't get better without treatment.
Depression isn't the only condition after birth, and it doesn't always look like sadness. Feeling angry, irritable or moody can be a sign too.
bullets: Anxiety: constant worry, a feeling that something bad is about to happen, racing thoughts, trouble sitting still, or physical symptoms like dizziness, hot flashes or nausea.

Postpartum OCD: upsetting thoughts or images about your baby that keep coming back, and urges to clean, check or count to calm them. Moms with OCD are disturbed by these thoughts and are very unlikely to act on them, and treatment helps.
Postpartum psychosis is rare and an emergency: seeing or hearing things that aren't there, strange beliefs, or confusion. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.

sections.heading: How treatment can help
paragraphs: Talk therapy, medicine, or both can help. Ask your provider which options fit you, including if you're breastfeeding. Your OB-GYN, midwife, your baby's pediatrician or your own doctor can help you find care. You can bring it up at any visit, including your baby's checkups.
It can help to tell one trusted person how you're really doing, and to write down what you're feeling to share with your provider.

sections.heading: Who am I now? The identity shift
paragraphs: Many moms feel a quiet grief for the person they were before the baby: their freedom, their body, their work, their time. Some people call this transition matrescence.
You can love your baby deeply and still miss your old life. Both can be true at the same time.
Your new self is still being built. Small things that feel like you, like a walk, a song, a call with a friend or ten quiet minutes, can help you find your way back to yourself.

sections.heading: Boundaries with well-meaning family
paragraphs: Visitors and advice usually come from love, but you're allowed to protect your rest, your recovery and your baby. A short, kind script makes it easier to say no.
bullets: "We're not having visitors yet. We'll let you know when we're ready."
"Thanks for the tip. We're following our pediatrician's advice on that."
"It would really help if you could bring dinner or fold some laundry while you're here."
"Please wash your hands before you hold the baby."
"We'd love a short visit. Can we say an hour?"
Ask your partner to pass on the message to their side of the family, so you don't have to.

sections.heading: You and your partner
paragraphs: Most couples find the first months hard. Less sleep, new roles and an uneven load can lead to resentment, even in strong relationships.
Talk about the work, not just the feelings. Make the invisible tasks visible, like booking appointments, buying diapers or planning meals, and split them in a way that feels fair to both of you.
bullets: Take sleep shifts so each of you gets one longer stretch of rest.
Check in for five minutes a day: "What was hardest today? What do you need tomorrow?"
Name small things you appreciate in each other.
Partners can have postpartum depression and anxiety too. Encourage each other to get support.
If the stress feels like too much, a couples or family therapist can help.

articles.title: Practical life and mom hacks
articles.summary: [PLACEHOLDER - needs expert review] Saving time and sanity when every minute counts: comfy clothes, easy meals, and your first outings with a newborn.

sections.heading: Clothes that fit the body you have now
paragraphs: Your body keeps changing for months after birth, and that's normal. You don't need a new wardrobe, just a few comfortable pieces that make you feel like yourself again.

If you had a C-section, soft high-waisted bottoms that sit above the incision, or low ones that sit well below it, are often more comfortable than waistbands that press on it. Ask your provider before using a belly band or support garment.
bullets: Soft, stretchy leggings or joggers with a wide waistband
Button-front or wrap tops, and nursing tops or bras if you're breastfeeding
Breathable cotton underwear in a size up while you heal
A long cardigan or overshirt that goes over everything
Slip-on shoes, for when bending down feels like a lot
One outfit you love, for days you want to feel put together

sections.heading: Easy, nourishing meals
paragraphs: When your hands are full, food that's ready in minutes makes a big difference. A little planning, or a friend's help, can stock your freezer before or after the baby arrives.
bullets: Freeze soups, chilis, curries and casseroles in single portions, labeled with the name and date.
Cool cooked food and put it in the fridge or freezer within 2 hours.
Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Frozen meals taste best within 3 to 4 months.
Thaw frozen meals in the fridge, in cold water, or in the microwave, never on the counter.
Reheat leftovers until they're steaming hot, to 165°F.
Keep one-handed snacks within reach: cheese sticks, yogurt, fruit, nut butter on toast, trail mix, energy bites and hard-boiled eggs.
Keep a water bottle wherever you usually feed the baby.

sections.heading: Grocery shortcuts
paragraphs: Grocery delivery or curbside pickup can save hours a week. Keep a running list of staples in your notes app so reordering takes a minute.
When friends ask how they can help, it's okay to say: "A meal or a grocery run would be amazing."
bullets: Stock up on staples: frozen vegetables, canned beans, rice, pasta, oats, eggs and bread.
Pre-cut fruit and vegetables cost a bit more but save time on hard days.
Rotisserie chicken turns into sandwiches, salads, wraps and quesadillas.

sections.heading: Your first outings with a newborn
paragraphs: Leaving the house for the first time can feel huge. Start small: a short walk around the block, a quick coffee, or a visit to a friend. Each trip gets easier.
Go at a time that's usually calm for your baby, often right after a feed. Know where you could sit to feed or change them, and give yourself permission to head home early.
bullets: In the car, babies ride rear-facing in their car seat, with the harness snug and no bulky coat underneath. Lay a blanket over the buckled straps instead.
Car seats are for travel, not for sleeping or feeding outside the car.
Keep babies younger than 6 months out of direct sun. Use shade, light clothing that covers their arms and legs, and a wide-brimmed hat. Sunscreen is a last resort, on small areas like the face.
Wash your hands, and ask others to wash theirs, before touching the baby.

sections.heading: Packing the diaper bag
paragraphs: Restock the bag as soon as you get home, so it's always ready to grab.
bullets: Diapers (one for every 2 hours you'll be out, plus 2 extra) and wipes
A changing pad and a few bags for dirty diapers or clothes
A spare outfit for the baby, and a spare top for you
Burp cloths
Feeding supplies: a nursing cover if you like one, or bottles and formula or pumped milk
A pacifier, if your baby uses one
A hat and a light blanket
Hand sanitizer and tissues
Water, a snack and a phone charger for you
Your baby's insurance card and pediatrician's number
